name: Firefly Aerospace Inc.

profile.description: Firefly Aerospace Inc. is a space and defense technology company offering launch (Alpha rocket), lunar landers (Blue Ghost), spacecraft solutions, and in-space services. Q2 2026 revenue rose 657% to $117.7M, beating the $88.7M consensus, driven largely by an acquired business in Spacecraft Solutions; first-half 2026 revenue was $198.6M versus $71.4M a year earlier. Management guided FY2026 revenue to $420-450M in March 2026 and reported backlog of about $1.3B at Q1 2026. CEO Jason Kim, formerly CEO of Boeing's Millennium Space Systems, has led the company since October 2024. Q3 2026 results had not been reported as of the screen date.

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (2/3): Firefly expanded from small-launch into lunar landers and spacecraft, achieving a commercial Moon landing with Blue Ghost and a 27-hour responsive national-security launch [5], and added an acquired spacecraft business that grew the segment by $99.1M (+1,077%) in Q2 2026 [1]. But four of Alpha's six flights have failed, including the loss of the Flight 7 first stage in September 2025 [6]. AI Deployment (1/2): Firefly promotes AI-enabled autonomous guidance work [5], but discloses no AI revenue or quantified savings. Market Share (1/2): Firefly is one of few US providers with both launch and lunar-landing capability, but it is a small player next to SpaceX and Rocket Lab. Pipeline (1/2): FY2026 revenue guidance of $420-450M and a ~$1.3-1.5B backlog give visibility [1][2], but no new product launches with dates were confirmed in this research. R&D Intensity (1/1): 2025 R&D of $200.1M was 125% of $159.9M revenue [4], far above the aerospace norm.

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): Firefly frames its work as providing responsive access to space so customers can 'launch, land, and orbit' [5], a clear statement of what it does but not a distinctive deeper purpose. Community Impact (0/2): No significant charitable or community programs were found. Employee Retention (0/2): No turnover or tenure data was found, and the prior CEO left in 2024 amid reports of an inappropriate relationship with an employee [3]. Insider Buying (0/2): Insider activity has been net selling, including a large secondary sale by sponsor AE Industrial Partners [5].

infrastructure.label: WEAK
infrastructure.analysis: Calculated mechanically on the Growth weighting (raw 3.33/10), on available metrics only because the 5-year revenue CAGR and PEG are unavailable for this 2025 IPO with negative forward earnings [2][4]. A near-zero D/E of 4.4% and 657% quarterly revenue growth score full marks. ROE of -58%, a -129% profit margin, and a negative forward P/E of -10.0 all score zero [2]. Liquidity is sufficient at about $53M of daily dollar volume.

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (8/9): Firefly builds and flies rockets, lunar landers, and spacecraft for NASA and the Defense Department, physical, regulated work that AI cannot substitute [3][5]. AI is more likely an enabler, through autonomous guidance and faster engineering, and CEO Kim has said demand for launch outpaces available rocket capacity [3]. AI Opportunity (0/1): No quantifiable AI-derived revenue is disclosed [1].

infinite_game.summary: Through Sinek's lens, Firefly is an ambitious young company that has already survived bankruptcy and a CEO scandal, but its identity is still defined by contracts and launch cadence rather than a Just Cause. Repeated Alpha failures, IPO-disclosure litigation, and sponsor selling make it look like a finite player racing for scale.

just_cause.analysis: Firefly's language about responsive space access and lunar exploration has some aspiration, but it reads as a capability pitch rather than a vision of a future people would sacrifice for [5]. Strategy is driven by government contract wins and revenue guidance [1].

trusting_teams.analysis: The previous CEO departed in mid-2024 amid reports of an inappropriate relationship with an employee [3], and a securities class action alleges the company overstated Alpha readiness before its IPO [6]. No evidence of high trust or low turnover was found.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Firefly positions itself on speed and responsiveness against SpaceX and Rocket Lab [3]. No evidence was found of rivals being framed as benchmarks to learn from.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Firefly evolved from a launch-only startup into a multi-mission space company spanning lunar landers, spacecraft, and in-space services, and added an acquired spacecraft business [1][5]. These moves broaden the model, but the company is too young to have faced a true reinvention test.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Leadership kept spending heavily on R&D ($200M in 2025) and on automated composite manufacturing to scale launch, despite large losses [3][4]. The record of overstated readiness alleged in litigation and the Alpha failures temper this [6].

investment_thesis: Firefly is one of a handful of US companies with launch, lunar-landing, and spacecraft capability, and revenue is scaling fast: Q2 2026 revenue rose 657% to $117.7M and FY2026 guidance is $420-450M, supported by a backlog of about $1.3-1.5B [1][2]. Defense demand for responsive space and a nearly debt-free balance sheet (D/E 4.4%) give it room to keep investing [2].
thesis_continued: Profitability is distant (2025 net loss of $298M, R&D at 125% of revenue), four of six Alpha flights have failed, and much of 2026 growth comes from an acquisition rather than organic launch execution [1][4][6]. Weak Inspiration, a low Infrastructure score, and a finite Infinite Game profile hold the IOWN score at WATCH despite strong AI Resilience.
key_catalysts: Q3 2026 earnings and any update to the $420-450M FY2026 revenue guidance [1]
Successful Alpha return-to-flight missions that restore launch credibility after the 2025 failures [6]
Further defense and NASA awards building on the ~$1.3-1.5B backlog [1]
key_risks: Launch failures: four of six Alpha flights have failed, and the FAA grounded Alpha after the April 2025 failure [6]
Securities class action alleging the company overstated Alpha readiness and spacecraft demand at its IPO [6]
Heavy cash burn (2025 net loss $298M) and dependence on government contract timing [4]

backlog.note: Backlog grew from about $1.3B at Q1 2026 to a record ~$1.5B at Q2 2026, driven by government spacecraft, lunar, and defense awards [1]. Funded backlog and TTM book-to-bill are not disclosed. The ~12.7-quarter backlog-to-revenue ratio (vs. Q2 revenue of $117.7M) is very high, which signals execution and capacity risk as much as visibility.
